1310:
To automate something means to set up a task or process so that it runs on its own — without a person needing to do it manually each time.

Think of it this way: imagine you had to turn your bedroom light on every morning at 6 AM. Every single day, you'd have to wake up and flip the switch. Now imagine you connected that light to a timer that does it for you automatically. You set it up once, and from that point on, the light turns on by itself every morning. You just automated the task of switching on the light.

That is the essence of the word. You hand a repetitive job over to a machine, a system, or a program — and it takes care of that job on its own from then on.

To automate something is to design or configure a system so that it performs a task or series of tasks with little to no human involvement each time it runs. The human effort shifts from doing the task repeatedly to setting up the system once that will do it repeatedly.

The key elements are:

  • There is a task that would otherwise need a human to do it.
  • A machine, computer program, or mechanical system is set up to do that task instead.
  • The task then happens consistently and repeatedly, without someone manually triggering it every time.
Everyday examples to make it stick

At home: A washing machine automates the work of scrubbing clothes by hand. You load the clothes, choose a setting, press start — and the machine handles the rest. You didn't have to scrub, rinse, and wring clothes yourself.

In a kitchen: A bread maker automates bread baking. You add the ingredients, and the machine kneads, rests, and bakes on a timed cycle.

On a phone: When your phone automatically backs up your photos to the cloud every night, that backup process has been automated. Nobody presses a button each night — the system was configured once and runs on its own.

In offices: Instead of an employee manually sending a "Happy Birthday" email to each customer on their birthday, a company can automate it — a program checks birthdays daily and sends the emails without anyone lifting a finger.

In factories: Car manufacturers automate the welding of car parts. Robotic arms do the welding thousands of times a day, consistently and precisely, replacing the need for a human to weld each joint by hand.
The important nuance: "little to no" human involvement

Automating something doesn't always mean humans disappear from the picture entirely. It means the repetitive, manual effort is removed or drastically reduced.

For example, a pilot can automate the plane's cruising through autopilot — the system holds the altitude, speed, and direction. But a human pilot still takes off, lands, and monitors everything. The tedious, constant task of manually adjusting controls during a long flight has been automated, even though humans are still involved.

This is an important point: automation handles the routine, repeated parts of a task. Humans often still make decisions, handle exceptions, or manage the system itself.

Understanding why people automate things helps you understand the word more deeply.

To save time. If you have to send the same report to your manager every Monday, you could automate it so the report is generated and sent automatically. You get those hours back.

To reduce human error. Humans get tired, distracted, and make mistakes — especially on repetitive tasks. A machine doing the same task over and over will do it the same way every time. Automating a process makes it more consistent and reliable.

To handle scale. A human can personally reply to 20 emails a day. But a business that gets 50,000 customer emails a day cannot hire enough people to respond to all of them. By automating responses to common questions, they can handle that scale.

To free up human time for better things. When you automate routine, low-thinking tasks, people are freed to focus on creative, strategic, or complex work that genuinely needs a human mind.
How the word is used in sentences

The verb "automate" is used simply and directly. Here are natural examples:

  • "The company automated its payroll system." → The company set up a system so employees are paid automatically each month without someone manually processing each payment.
  • "She automated her social media posts." → She scheduled posts using a tool that publishes them automatically at set times, rather than her logging in each time to post manually.
  • "They are trying to automate the data entry process." → They are working on getting a program to enter data on its own, instead of having staff type it in manually.
  • "This software automates repetitive tasks." → This software is designed to handle tasks that would otherwise be done by hand over and over again.
  • "The factory automated its production line in 2020." → The factory replaced manual labor on the production line with machines that now do the work automatically.
The related forms of the word (they help round out your understanding)

• Automated (adjective): describes something that has already been set up to run on its own. "An automated system." "An automated response."
  • Automation (noun): the concept, process, or result of making things run automatically. "Automation is changing the job market." "The automation of manufacturing."
  • Automatic (adjective): describes something that works on its own, often as a built-in feature. "The car has an automatic transmission."

The difference between automatic and automated is subtle but worth knowing: something automatic tends to work on its own by its very design (like an automatic door that opens when you approach it). Something automated was deliberately set up or programmed by someone to run without manual effort (like an automated email sequence a marketer built).

To automate is to make something work by itself. You replace the need for manual, repeated human action with a system — mechanical or digital — that takes over. The goal is always the same: less human effort on routine work, more consistency, more speed, and more scale.

Once you've automated something, it runs in the background, doing its job, while you move on to other things. That's the power — and the appeal — of the word.
1311:
"Automatically" means in a way that happens by itself, without someone needing to do it manually or think about it each time.

The key idea is the absence of deliberate, repeated human effort. Once a system, rule, or habit is in place, the action simply happens on its own.

This word lives in two very different situations, but both share the same soul — something running without active human involvement.

1. Machines, Systems, and Programs

This is the most common use today. When a machine, app, computer, or system is set up to do something without a person pressing a button or giving a command each time, it does that thing automatically.

  • "The streetlights turn on automatically at sunset." (A sensor detects darkness and triggers the lights — you don't flip a switch.)
  • "My phone automatically saves photos to the cloud." (You set it up once; after that, it just happens on its own.)
  • "The washing machine automatically stops when the cycle is done."
  • "If you don't log out, the website will automatically log you out after 30 minutes."

In all these cases, a rule or program was built in advance. When the right condition arrives, the action fires — no human needed at that moment.

2. Human Behavior, Habits, and Reflexes

Humans also do things automatically — meaning without consciously deciding to do them, because the action has become so natural, practiced, or instinctive that it requires no active thought.

  • "When a ball flew toward his face, he automatically closed his eyes." (He didn't think "I should close my eyes" — it just happened.)
  • "After years of driving, she automatically checks her mirrors before changing lanes."
  • "He automatically reached for his phone every time he felt bored."
  • "When the teacher asked a question, the student automatically raised her hand."

Here, "automatically" describes the body or mind acting from deep habit, reflex, or training — bypassing conscious decision-making.
The Hidden Ingredient: A Prior Setup

One of the most important things to understand about "automatically" is that it does not mean something happens for no reason or by magic. There is always something that was set up beforehand — a program was written, a rule was created, or a habit was formed. "Automatically" describes the execution, not the origin.

Think of it like a mousetrap. You set it up once. After that, when a mouse steps on it, it snaps automatically — you don't need to be there, watching and deciding to close it each time. The trap does the work.

  • A thermostat automatically turns on the heater — because someone set a temperature target.
  • Your email automatically filters spam — because filters were configured.
  • A musician's fingers automatically find the right notes — because they practiced thousands of times.

Remove the prior setup, and nothing happens "automatically." The word always implies: someone or something prepared this in advance, so that future executions need no extra effort.
"Automatically" Also Carries a Sense of Certainty and Inevitability

Beyond machines and habits, "automatically" is also used to say that something will necessarily and certainly happen as a direct result of something else — like a rule that executes itself without anyone having to make a fresh decision.

  • "If you score below 40%, you are automatically disqualified."
  • "Paying the fee automatically renews your membership."
  • "Employees who work more than five years automatically qualify for a pension."

In these sentences, there is no room for a human to step in and decide case by case. The rule has already been decided. The outcome follows automatically — without negotiation, without effort, without someone having to say "okay, disqualify this person." The system does it.

This sense of the word carries a slightly formal tone and is very common in rules, laws, policies, and agreements.

The cleanest way to sharpen your understanding of "automatically" is to contrast it with its opposite: manually.

  • "Manually" = you have to do it yourself, each time, with deliberate effort.
  • "Automatically" = the system, machine, or habit does it for you, without you acting each time.
Manual: You water your plants every morning yourself.Automatic: A timer-controlled drip system waters them automatically.
Manual: You save your document by pressing Ctrl+S.Automatic: The app automatically saves every two minutes.
Manual: A security guard checks each ID at the door.Automatic: A scanner automatically reads and verifies each ID.

Whenever you see "automatically," ask: What would someone have to do manually if this weren't automatic? That will reveal exactly what effort is being eliminated.
How It Feels in a Sentence

"Automatically" always answers the question "How does it happen?" It is an adverb, so it describes the manner of an action — specifically telling you that the action occurs on its own, without deliberate effort each time.

It usually sits close to the verb it describes:

  • "The fan starts automatically."
  • "She automatically ducked when she heard the sound."
  • "The discount is applied automatically at checkout."
  • "The file was automatically deleted after seven days."

"Automatically" ≠ "instantly"
Something can happen automatically but still take time. Your phone automatically backs up at night — it happens without your involvement, but it takes 20 minutes. "Automatically" is about who (or what) does the work, not about speed.

"Automatically" ≠ "always"
Automatic things happen when their conditions are met, not necessarily at all times. The sprinklers turn on automatically at 6 a.m. — but only at 6 a.m., not every minute of the day.

"Automatically" ≠ "perfectly"
Automatic does not mean error-free. Spam filters automatically move emails — but they sometimes make mistakes and move legitimate emails too. The automatic nature of the action doesn't guarantee accuracy.
A Complete Picture in One Sentence

If you had to remember just one definition: "Automatically" means in a way that happens by itself, driven by a pre-set system, rule, or deeply ingrained habit — without someone needing to actively decide or act each time it occurs.

1. Machines/systems: A device or program does something on its own, without human action each time. (The door opens automatically.)
  2. Human habits/reflexes: A person does something without conscious thought, out of instinct or deep practice. (She automatically knew the answer.)
  3. Rules and consequences: A result follows as a guaranteed, inevitable outcome of a condition — no one has to make a fresh decision. (You are automatically enrolled when you sign up.)

All three meanings share the same core: no active, repeated effort required — it just happens.
1312:
Automation is the use of technology — such as machines, software, or systems — to perform tasks on their own, with little or no human effort required each time. Once an automated system is set up, it does the work by itself, following instructions that were given to it in advance.

The soul of the word is self-operation. When something is automated, it doesn't wait for a person to tell it what to do every single time. It already knows what to do, and it does it.
A Simple Example to Lock It In

Imagine you need to water your garden every morning. You could go outside with a watering can every day — that requires your effort, your time, and your presence each time. Now imagine you install a system of sprinklers connected to a timer. You set it once: "Turn on at 7 AM, run for 10 minutes, turn off." From that point on, the sprinklers do it automatically — every morning, without you lifting a finger.

That is automation. You replaced a repeated human action with a system that handles it on its own.

For something to truly count as automation, a few things are happening under the hood:

Pre-set instructions. The system is given a set of rules or commands in advance. It follows those rules every time a certain condition is met. A thermostat, for example, is programmed with one rule: "If the room temperature drops below 68°F, turn on the heater." It checks this constantly and acts on its own.

Sensing or triggering. Automated systems often detect something — a temperature, a time, a signal, a user action — and use that as a trigger to begin working. The detection happens without a human having to notice it and respond.

Reduced or eliminated human involvement. This is the defining result. A human may be needed to set up the system or fix it when it breaks, but they are not needed to actually perform the repeated task itself. That's the whole point.
The Spectrum: From Simple to Complex

Automation isn't just one thing. It exists on a wide spectrum, from very simple to remarkably sophisticated.

At the simple end, you have fixed automation — systems designed to do one specific task, over and over, without any variation. A factory machine that stamps a metal part into the same shape thousands of times a day is a good example. It can't do anything else, but it does that one thing perfectly and tirelessly.

In the middle, you have programmable automation — systems that can be reprogrammed to do different tasks. A machine in a manufacturing plant might be reprogrammed to produce a different product when needed. It still follows rigid instructions, but those instructions can be changed.

Further along, there is flexible automation — systems that can handle some variation on their own. A sorting machine at a warehouse might be able to handle packages of different shapes and sizes and route each one to the correct location. It adapts to variation without needing to be stopped and reprogrammed.

At the advanced end, there is intelligent automation, where artificial intelligence is involved. Here, the system doesn't just follow rules — it can learn from data, recognize patterns, make judgments, and handle situations it wasn't explicitly programmed for. A spam filter in your email is a simple example: it learns what spam looks like and automatically sorts your inbox. A self-driving car is a more complex one: it perceives the world around it in real time and makes driving decisions on its own.
Where Automation Shows Up in Everyday Life

Once you know what automation is, you'll start seeing it everywhere.

In your home, your washing machine automates what used to be hours of hand-washing laundry. Your phone's auto-correct automates the process of fixing spelling errors as you type. A smart thermostat automates climate control based on your schedule and preferences.

In banking, automatic bill payments mean your electricity bill gets paid on the due date without you writing a check. ATMs automated what bank tellers used to do manually.

In industry, car factories use robotic arms that weld, paint, and assemble vehicles with far greater speed and precision than human workers could manage at that scale. Automated conveyor belts, sorting machines, and inventory systems keep warehouses running around the clock.

In healthcare, machines automatically monitor a patient's heart rate, oxygen levels, and blood pressure, and alert medical staff the moment something goes out of range — without a nurse having to constantly watch a screen.

In agriculture, automated irrigation systems detect soil moisture levels and deliver exactly the right amount of water to crops, saving water and labor.

In software, businesses use tools that automatically send a welcome email when someone signs up for a service, generate reports at the end of each day, or back up data every night at midnight.
What Automation Is Not: Clearing Up a Common Confusion

Automation is not the same as mechanization, though the two are closely related and often confused.

Mechanization means using machines to help humans do work — but a human is still actively operating the machine and guiding it. A person driving a forklift is mechanized work: the forklift makes lifting heavy things possible, but the human is in control every step of the way.

Automation takes it further: the forklift navigates the warehouse on its own, determines where to go, picks up the correct pallet, and delivers it — without a human in the driver's seat.

The dividing line is this: in mechanization, the human is doing the task with the help of a machine. In automation, the machine is doing the task on its own.

The reason automation is one of the most important concepts in the modern world comes down to a few powerful advantages it offers.

Speed. Machines can work far faster than humans. A machine that stamps metal parts can produce thousands per hour. A human cannot.

Consistency and accuracy. Machines don't get tired, distracted, or bored. A human performing a repetitive task for eight hours will make mistakes as the day wears on. An automated system performs the 10,000th repetition with the same precision as the first.

Availability. Automated systems can run 24 hours a day, seven days a week. They don't need sleep, lunch breaks, or weekends.

Scale. Automation makes it possible to do things at a scale that would be impossible with human labor alone. A single automated system can process millions of transactions, emails, or data records in a day.

Safety. Automation can take over tasks that are dangerous for humans — working in extreme heat, handling toxic chemicals, mining deep underground, or defusing explosives.

Automation is not without its downsides, and it would be incomplete not to mention them.

Job displacement is the most widely discussed concern. When machines take over tasks that humans used to do, those humans can lose their jobs. This has happened repeatedly throughout history — first in agriculture, then in manufacturing, and now increasingly in services and knowledge work. Automation creates new types of jobs too, but the transition can be painful for workers whose specific skills are no longer needed.

High upfront cost. Setting up automated systems — buying the equipment, writing the software, integrating everything — is expensive. Smaller businesses sometimes can't afford it, which can create unequal competitive advantages.

Rigidity in unexpected situations. Most automated systems are only as good as the instructions they were given. When something unusual happens — something outside what the designers anticipated — automated systems can fail badly, sometimes in ways a human would never fail. A self-checkout machine can't handle a grocery item that has no barcode. A human cashier can.

Dependence and fragility. When an organization relies heavily on automation, a breakdown in the automated system can halt everything. The more automated a process is, the more catastrophic a failure in that system can become.

Ethical questions. As automation becomes more intelligent — using AI to make decisions that affect people's lives, such as hiring decisions, loan approvals, or medical diagnoses — serious ethical questions arise about fairness, accountability, and the role of human judgment.

Today, automation has expanded far beyond physical machines in factories. Software automation — often called digital automation or robotic process automation (RPA) — involves software programs that handle repetitive computer-based tasks. A program might automatically extract data from one system and enter it into another, generate invoices, or process insurance claims, all without a human touching it.

Artificial intelligence has pushed the frontier even further. Modern automation can now handle tasks that require judgment, pattern recognition, and even creativity — things that were once thought to be exclusively human territory. AI can write first drafts of text, diagnose diseases from medical scans, detect fraud in financial transactions, and recommend what you should watch next on a streaming platform.

This makes automation in the 21st century qualitatively different from what it was in the 20th. It no longer just replaces physical, repetitive labor. It is beginning to assist — and in some cases replace — cognitive, decision-making work as well. This is why automation is one of the most consequential and debated forces shaping the economy, work, and society today.

If you had to carry one sentence with you, let it be this: Automation is when a system is designed to do a task by itself — repeatedly, reliably, and without needing a human to actively perform it each time.

Everything else — the machines, the software, the AI, the factory robots, the smart thermostat — is just automation showing up in different forms, in different places, at different levels of sophistication.
1313:
An automaton is anything — a machine, a device, or even a person — that operates on its own, carrying out a set of actions automatically, without needing a human to guide it step by step in real time. The defining quality of an automaton is that its behavior is pre-determined: it follows a fixed set of rules or instructions that were built into it in advance, and it executes those rules on its own.

Think of it this way: if you wind up a toy and it walks across the floor by itself, that toy is behaving like an automaton. You set it in motion, and it does the rest without you.
The Three Main Contexts Where This Word Is Used

1. A Self-Operating Mechanical Machine (the original and most common meaning)

Historically, an automaton refers to a physical, mechanical machine — often one built to imitate the movements of a living creature, especially a human being or an animal. These were built with gears, springs, levers, and clockwork mechanisms, and they could perform impressive, lifelike actions entirely on their own once set in motion.

Famous historical examples include 18th-century mechanical marvels like a duck that appeared to eat grain and digest it, or a figure that could write with a pen. These were not toys — they were extraordinary feats of engineering. The key point is that every motion was pre-programmed into the machinery itself. The machine did not think, did not react to its environment, and did not make decisions. It just executed its built-in sequence, over and over.

In modern use, the word automaton can be extended to robots and automated machines that work through pre-set instructions — for instance, a factory robot that welds car parts by repeatedly performing the exact same set of movements.

The critical distinction: an automaton is not the same thing as an intelligent machine. A true automaton does not think or adapt. It simply runs through its sequence. If you place an obstacle in the path of a clockwork walking figure, it will walk right into it, because it has no awareness. It is purely mechanical obedience to its own programming.

2. A Person Who Acts Like a Machine (the figurative meaning)

When the word is used to describe a person, it is almost always figurative — and usually critical or sad in tone. Calling someone an automaton means they are going through life, work, or actions in a robotic, unthinking, emotionless way, as if they have no inner life, no independent judgment, and no personal feeling. They just do what they are told or what habit demands, again and again, without questioning, reflecting, or feeling.

For example: "After twenty years in the same job, doing the same tasks every single day, he had become a mere automaton — clocking in, completing his tasks, clocking out, with no real engagement or thought."

This usage highlights something deeply human: we expect people to think, feel, and choose. When someone completely surrenders all of that and merely executes a routine, we describe them with this word to show that they have, in a way, stopped being fully human in their behavior.

3. An Abstract Mathematical Model (the technical/computer science meaning)

In mathematics and computer science, the word has a very precise, specialized meaning that is related to the general idea but is far more abstract. Here, an automaton is not a physical machine at all — it is a theoretical model used to describe and study how computation and logic work.

In this context, an automaton is imagined as a system that can exist in different states and that moves from one state to another based on inputs it receives, following transition rules that tell it exactly what to do in every situation.

Picture a simple turnstile at a subway entrance. It has two states: locked and unlocked. If it is locked and you push it, it stays locked. If it is locked and you insert a coin, it moves to unlocked. If it is unlocked and you push through, it goes back to locked. That turnstile is a perfect real-world model of an automaton — a system with defined states, defined inputs, and defined rules for moving between states.

Computer scientists use automata (the plural) to model how programs process language, how compilers understand code, how search engines match patterns, and much more. Different types of automata have different levels of power and capability — the simplest being a finite automaton (limited memory, fixed states), and the most powerful theoretical one being a Turing machine, which is essentially an abstract model of any computer that can ever exist.

This technical meaning is what you will encounter in university-level mathematics, computer science, and linguistics courses.

The word has two accepted plurals. Automata is the classical plural (borrowed from the original Greek form) and is strongly preferred in formal, technical, and academic contexts — especially in computer science, where you will almost always see "automata theory" rather than "automatons theory." Automatons is the regular English plural and is perfectly correct in everyday use when speaking about mechanical machines or people.

This is a word that carries a certain weight to it. It is not a neutral, purely descriptive word like "machine" or "device." It tends to carry one of two feelings depending on context:

Wonder and admiration — when used about historical or mechanical automata, there is often a sense of awe. A beautifully crafted 18th-century mechanical figure that can draw a portrait entirely on its own feels magical and astonishing. The word in this context evokes craftsmanship and ingenuity.

Coldness or dehumanization — when used about a person or about modern repetitive systems, the word tends to feel bleak or critical. It implies a loss of humanity, spontaneity, or thought. Nobody wants to be called an automaton. It suggests that something essential about being alive — the capacity to think, feel, and choose — has been switched off or suppressed.

Automaton means: a self-operating entity — mechanical, human, or theoretical — that follows pre-set rules and carries out actions automatically, without real-time human guidance, genuine thought, or independent decision-making.

Whether it is a 300-year-old clockwork musician that plays a flute by itself, a factory robot repeating the same weld ten thousand times a day, a person who goes through life on pure habit and routine, or an abstract mathematical model of computation — the word automaton captures the same essential quality in all of them: automatic, rule-driven action, with no genuine thinking or feeling behind it.
1314:
Autonomous means self-governing — able to make your own rules, decisions, and choices, and act on them freely, without being controlled or directed by an outside force.

Break the word down in your mind this way: auto = self, nomos = law. So autonomous literally captures the idea of "being a law unto yourself." You set your own rules. You direct yourself.
The Simplest Way to Understand It

Imagine two employees at a company.

Employee A is told exactly what to do every hour. Their manager decides their tasks, their schedule, and how they should handle every situation. They follow instructions. They have no say.

Employee B is given a goal — "make our customers happy" — and then left entirely to figure out how to do it. They decide their own schedule, their own methods, and handle problems their own way. Nobody is standing over them giving orders.

Employee B is autonomous. They are self-directed. They function on their own judgment.

That gap — the difference between being told what to do versus deciding for yourself — is exactly what autonomous captures.
What It Really Means, Layer by Layer

1. Independence from outside control

The most fundamental meaning: an autonomous person, group, or system is not controlled, commanded, or dictated to by an external authority. The rules and decisions come from within, not from outside.

This is the heart of the word. Everything else is a specific application of this idea.

2. Self-direction

Being autonomous doesn't just mean being free from control — it means being capable of directing yourself. A dog that escapes its leash is free, but it isn't autonomous in the true sense. An autonomous entity has its own internal mechanism for making decisions — whether that's a human's mind, a government's constitution, or a robot's programming.

3. Degree — it's not always all-or-nothing

Autonomy exists on a spectrum. Something can be partially autonomous (makes some decisions independently but is still overseen or constrained in others) or fully autonomous (operates entirely on its own). You'll often hear phrases like "greater autonomy" or "limited autonomy" for this reason.
How "Autonomous" Is Used in Different Areas of Life

The word is used widely across many fields, and the core meaning stays the same — only the subject changes.

People and individuals

A person described as autonomous makes their own life choices — what to believe, how to live, what values to follow — without being pressured, manipulated, or controlled by others. An autonomous individual thinks for themselves. They are not blindly obedient to a religion, a group, a parent, or a government. They reason things through and act on their own conclusions.

"She was a deeply autonomous thinker who never accepted ideas just because others told her to."

Countries and regions

A country or region is autonomous when it governs itself — it has its own laws, its own leadership, and its own decision-making power, rather than being ruled by another country or a central authority.

A good example: a semi-autonomous region within a country has some freedom to govern itself (its own local laws, perhaps its own parliament), but is still ultimately part of and accountable to a larger nation. It is partially but not fully autonomous.

"The autonomous region had its own legislature but still fell under the national constitution."

Machines and technology

This is one of the most common modern uses. An autonomous machine (a robot, a car, a drone, a software system) operates without needing a human to control it in real time. It senses its environment, makes decisions, and takes actions on its own.

A self-driving car is autonomous — no human is steering it, braking it, or telling it when to turn. It handles all of that itself.

"The autonomous drone mapped the entire forest without a single human command after takeoff."

Organizations and institutions

A school, hospital, company, or any institution can be described as autonomous when it runs its own affairs — setting its own policies, budget, and internal rules — without being micromanaged by a higher authority.

"The university was autonomous, free to design its own curriculum without government interference."

Biology and the body

In biology, autonomous refers to bodily processes that happen on their own, without you consciously controlling them. Your heart beats, your lungs breathe, your pupils adjust to light — all autonomously. The part of your nervous system that manages these is even called the autonomic nervous system (a closely related word).

Getting the edges of a word right is just as important as getting the center.

  • Autonomous ≠ Isolated. An autonomous person or country can still work with others, have relationships, and cooperate — they just aren't controlled by others. Independence of decision doesn't mean living in a bubble.
  • Autonomous ≠ Selfish or reckless. Autonomous doesn't imply someone does whatever they want with no regard for anyone else. It simply means the decision-making authority rests with them. They can still choose to be considerate, follow laws, or work within a framework — the point is they're doing so by their own choice, not because someone is forcing them.
  • Autonomous ≠ Automatic. These two words are often confused. Automatic means something happens mechanically, triggered by a condition — like an automatic door that opens when you step on a sensor. Autonomous implies a higher level: judgment, decision-making, and adapting to new situations. All autonomous machines are somewhat automatic, but not all automatic machines are autonomous.

When you call something or someone autonomous, you are making a statement about where the power and control lives. If it lives inside — in the person's own mind, in the region's own government, in the machine's own system — then the word fits. If the power lives outside, with someone else pulling the strings, then autonomous is the wrong word.

Think of it as a dial. On one end: total control by an outside force (a puppet, a colony, a remote-controlled drone). On the other end: complete self-governance (a fully independent person, a sovereign nation, a fully self-driving vehicle). Autonomous describes entities that sit toward the self-governing end of that dial.

• "The children were encouraged to become autonomous learners who could teach themselves."
  • "After years of occupation, the territory finally became an autonomous state."
  • "The factory now uses autonomous robots that require no human supervision on the floor."
  • "She valued her autonomous lifestyle and made every major decision without consulting others."
  • "The committee operated as an autonomous body, reporting to no one."

Autonomous describes anything — a person, group, region, or machine — that governs, directs, and controls itself from within, rather than being directed or controlled by an outside authority.

Once you hold that idea clearly, every use of the word across every field will make immediate, intuitive sense.
1315:
Autonomy means the freedom and ability to govern yourself — to make your own choices, live by your own rules, and direct your own life without being controlled by someone else.

Think of it this way: when you decide what to eat, what to believe, or how to spend your day without anyone forcing you otherwise, you are exercising autonomy. It is the opposite of being told what to do, having your decisions made for you, or being under someone else's control.

The single clearest way to remember it: autonomy = self-rule.

Autonomy is not just about doing whatever you want. It has two important ingredients working together:

Freedom from external control. Nobody is forcing you, pressuring you, or making decisions on your behalf. You are not a puppet. You are not blindly obeying orders. You are free from domination by outside forces.

The ability to actually decide for yourself. You have the inner capacity — the knowledge, the awareness, the mental clarity — to think through your situation and make a genuine, informed choice. A person locked in a room has no autonomy even if no one is shouting orders at them, because their freedom is taken away structurally.

True autonomy requires both. Freedom without the capacity to choose wisely is hollow. And the capacity to choose without freedom is useless.
How Autonomy Is Used in Different Areas of Life

This word shows up across many fields, and while the core meaning stays the same, each field emphasizes a slightly different angle of it.

In everyday personal life, autonomy refers to an individual's right to run their own life — to choose their career, their relationships, their values, their lifestyle — without others imposing their will on them. When a parent gradually lets a growing child make their own decisions, they are giving the child more autonomy. When a controlling partner dictates every move of their significant other, they are destroying that person's autonomy.

In politics and governance, autonomy refers to a region, group, or territory that has the right to govern itself to some degree, even if it is part of a larger country. For example, a region might have its own local government, its own laws, and its own cultural policies — that region has autonomy. It is not fully independent (that would be called sovereignty or independence), but it is not fully controlled from above either. It sits somewhere in between: self-governing within limits set by a larger authority.

In philosophy, autonomy is one of the most important concepts in ethics. The key question philosophers ask is: are you acting according to your own rational values and principles, or are you simply reacting to pressure, habit, emotion, or social expectation? A person with strong philosophical autonomy pauses, reflects, thinks critically, and then acts in line with values they have genuinely chosen for themselves — not values that were just handed to them or drilled into them without question.

In medicine and healthcare, patient autonomy is a foundational ethical principle. It means that a patient has the right to be fully informed about their condition and treatment options, and to make their own decisions about their own body — even if the doctor disagrees with that decision. A doctor cannot ethically force a treatment on a competent adult patient, because doing so would violate that patient's autonomy. This is why informed consent (the patient agreeing to a treatment after being properly informed) is such a big deal in medicine.

In the workplace, autonomy refers to how much freedom an employee has in deciding how to do their job — what approach to take, how to manage their time, and how to solve problems — without being micromanaged at every step. Research consistently shows that workers with more autonomy tend to be more motivated, more creative, and more satisfied with their jobs.

In psychology, autonomy is considered a fundamental human need. Psychologists who study motivation argue that people are at their happiest and most engaged when they feel they are choosing their actions freely, rather than being pressured or coerced. When autonomy is crushed, people often feel resentful, disengaged, or helpless.

In technology and artificial intelligence, an autonomous system (like a self-driving car or a drone) is one that operates and makes decisions on its own, without needing a human to control it at every step. The more it relies on itself to navigate situations, the more autonomous it is considered to be.

Autonomy is not an all-or-nothing thing. It exists on a spectrum.

A person, region, or system can have full autonomy (complete self-rule, no outside interference), partial autonomy (some self-rule, but with limits set by a higher authority), or very little autonomy (almost entirely controlled by an outside force).

For example, a child has very little autonomy early in life — parents make almost all decisions. As the child grows, they gain more and more autonomy. A fully functioning adult in a free society ideally has a high degree of personal autonomy. And even then, that autonomy has limits — your freedom ends where it begins to harm others. No society grants unlimited autonomy, because that would lead to chaos.

The direct opposite of autonomy is heteronomy — which simply means being ruled or controlled by an outside force rather than by yourself. While "heteronomy" is a technical term you may rarely encounter in casual conversation, the concept is everywhere: a worker who must do exactly what a boss says with no input, a colonized nation stripped of self-governance, or a person who makes every decision based on fear of what others think — all of these describe a lack of autonomy.

More commonly, you will hear autonomy contrasted with words like: control, dependence, obedience, submission, conformity, and coercion.

Autonomy is considered precious in most human societies because it is deeply tied to dignity and respect. To treat a person as autonomous is to acknowledge that they are a thinking, feeling, capable human being who deserves to make their own choices about their own life. To strip someone of autonomy is to treat them as an object, a tool, or a child who cannot be trusted.

This is why autonomy sits at the heart of major debates in law, ethics, politics, and medicine: Who gets to decide what happens to you? You, or someone else?

When autonomy is protected, people tend to flourish. When it is taken away — by authoritarian governments, abusive relationships, oppressive institutions, or paternalistic systems that treat adults like children — people suffer, even when those in control claim they are "doing it for their own good."

Autonomy is the state of being self-governing — having the freedom and the genuine capacity to make your own choices and live according to your own principles, rather than being controlled, directed, or decided for by someone else. It applies to individuals, groups, regions, institutions, and even machines. It exists on a spectrum (more or less, not just yes or no), and it is universally recognized as something deeply important to human dignity, freedom, and well-being.

An autopilot is a system — usually electronic or mechanical — that automatically controls a vehicle, keeping it on a steady course without the human operator having to do it manually, moment by moment.

Think of it this way: when you're riding a bicycle, you have to constantly balance, steer, and adjust. You can't let go for long. But imagine if the bicycle had a built-in system that kept itself perfectly balanced and pointed in the right direction on its own, while you simply watched. That built-in system would be the autopilot.

The word "autopilot" was born in aviation. Flying an aircraft requires constant, precise adjustments — to altitude, direction, and speed. On long flights, doing all of this manually, every second, would be exhausting for a pilot.

So engineers created a device — the autopilot — that handles these routine tasks automatically. The pilot sets the desired altitude, heading (direction), and speed, and the autopilot takes over, making tiny, continuous corrections to keep the aircraft on that exact path.

Crucially, the autopilot does not replace the pilot. The pilot is still there, monitoring everything, ready to take control. The autopilot simply removes the need for constant manual input, freeing the pilot's attention for more important decisions. Think of it as a highly skilled assistant, not a replacement.

Over time, the word "autopilot" spread to other vehicles and systems:

  • Ships use autopilots to hold a steady course across open water.
  • Spacecraft use autopilots to follow precise orbital paths.
  • Cars with modern cruise control or self-driving features are sometimes described as having autopilots (Tesla, for example, calls their driver-assistance feature "Autopilot").

In all these cases, the meaning is the same: a system that handles the routine job of controlling the vehicle automatically, so the human can step back.
The figurative meaning: Human behavior "on autopilot"

This is where the word gets its second — and equally important — life. In everyday English, "autopilot" (or the phrase "on autopilot") describes a state where a person is doing something automatically, without conscious thought or awareness.

Here's what that means in real life:

You wake up every morning and follow the same routine — brush teeth, make tea, get dressed. You've done it hundreds of times. Your body just does it. You're not really thinking about it. Your mind might be somewhere else entirely. That is being on autopilot. You are moving through familiar actions without active, deliberate attention.

Another example: A driver who has driven the same route to work for years might arrive and suddenly realize they can barely remember the drive. Their hands turned at the right corners, their foot braked at the right lights — all without conscious decision-making. They were on autopilot.
Is being on autopilot good or bad?

It depends on the situation, and this is an important nuance of the word.

It can be useful and efficient. Autopilot frees up mental energy. Because brushing your teeth requires no real thought, your mind can plan the day ahead. Skilled musicians, athletes, and surgeons often describe performing complex tasks "on autopilot" — meaning their training is so deep that the actions flow automatically, smoothly, and without effort. This is a sign of mastery.

It can also be a problem. If you're on autopilot when you should be paying attention, you make mistakes or miss things. A driver on autopilot might miss a road sign. A person eating on autopilot might not notice they're full. In these situations, being on autopilot means being absent-minded or mentally checked out.

So the word carries a quiet tension: autopilot is efficient, but it means you're not fully present.

• "The pilot engaged the autopilot after the plane reached cruising altitude."
    → Here, autopilot is the literal device on the aircraft.
  • "She was so tired that she ran on autopilot through the whole meeting."
    → Here, autopilot describes functioning without full conscious awareness.
  • "I need to snap out of autopilot and actually pay attention to what I'm eating."
    → Here, autopilot means a mindless, habitual state that the person wants to exit.
  • "Years of practice meant his fingers moved on autopilot across the piano keys."
    → Here, autopilot has a positive meaning — deep, effortless skill.

An autopilot is a system (in a vehicle) or a state (in a person) where things run automatically and without active, conscious control — useful for routine tasks, but a concern when full attention is actually needed.

An autopsy is a thorough, systematic medical examination of a dead human body, performed by a specially trained doctor, to find out why the person died, how they died, and what the state of their body was at the time of death.

Think of it this way: just as a doctor examines a living patient to understand what is wrong with them, an autopsy examines a dead body to understand what went wrong — and when, and how. It is essentially a scientific investigation of a body, on a body.

An autopsy is performed by a pathologist — a medical doctor who specializes in studying diseases, tissues, organs, and body fluids to understand the effects of illness and injury. When the death involves legal or criminal matters, a forensic pathologist (a pathologist with extra specialization in law-related deaths) typically takes over. These professionals work in hospitals, government offices called medical examiner's offices, or forensic laboratories. The official responsible for overseeing death investigations at a governmental level is called a medical examiner or a coroner, depending on the country or region.
What Actually Happens During an Autopsy

The process is careful, methodical, and conducted with professional dignity. It unfolds in several stages.

It begins with an external examination, where the doctor meticulously studies the outside of the entire body — looking for injuries, bruises, wounds, marks, or anything unusual on the skin, and noting the overall physical condition of the body.

Next comes the internal examination. The doctor makes a precise incision (typically a Y-shaped cut across the chest and down the abdomen) to access the body's internal organs. Each major organ — the heart, lungs, liver, brain, kidneys, spleen, and others — is carefully removed, weighed, visually inspected, and in many cases cut open further to look for abnormalities, disease, damage, or blockages.

After the visual examination, the process goes even deeper. Small pieces of tissue from various organs are collected and examined under a microscope — this is called histology or histopathological examination. It reveals things invisible to the naked eye, such as cellular damage, cancer, or infection at the microscopic level.

Additionally, blood, urine, and other body fluids are collected and sent to a laboratory for toxicology testing — a chemical analysis to detect the presence of drugs, alcohol, poisons, medications, or other substances in the body. Depending on the case, other tests such as microbiological cultures (to check for infections) or genetic testing may also be performed.

There are several distinct reasons an autopsy is carried out, and they each serve a different purpose.

To determine the cause and manner of death. The cause of death is the specific medical reason the person died — for example, a heart attack, a stroke, a drug overdose, or a stab wound. The manner of death is the broader legal and factual category it falls into: natural, accidental, suicide, homicide, or undetermined. The autopsy is the most reliable scientific method for establishing both, especially when they are not immediately obvious.

Legal and criminal investigations. When someone dies under suspicious circumstances — a possible murder, an unexplained sudden death, or a death involving potential negligence — law enforcement and legal authorities need hard, scientific evidence. The autopsy provides it. Its findings can be presented as formal evidence in a court of law, and the pathologist may even testify as an expert witness.

Medical understanding and quality of care. When a patient in a hospital dies from an illness, an autopsy can confirm whether the medical diagnosis made during their lifetime was accurate, reveal hidden conditions that were never detected, or show whether a treatment had any unexpected effects. This helps doctors learn and ultimately deliver better care to future patients.

Public health. If many people in a community are dying from an unknown or newly emerging disease, autopsies help scientists and public health officials identify what the disease is, how it damages the body, and how it spreads. This knowledge is essential for controlling outbreaks and protecting the wider population.

Family closure. Families who have lost a loved one often experience deep uncertainty and grief when the cause of death is unclear. An autopsy provides a definitive, science-backed answer to what happened, which can bring a degree of peace and closure.

Research and education. Autopsies have been a cornerstone of medical science for centuries. They are used in medical schools and research institutions to help students and scientists understand the human body, diseases, the effects of aging, and the long-term impacts of various medical treatments.
When is an Autopsy Typically Performed?

Autopsies are most commonly performed when a person dies suddenly without any known illness or explanation, when the death is violent or suspicious, when a young or otherwise healthy person dies for no obvious reason, when someone dies during or shortly after surgery, when a new or unknown disease may be involved, or when the death has legal significance. In many countries and jurisdictions, certain categories of death — such as homicide, suicide, or death in police custody — are required by law to undergo an autopsy, regardless of anyone's preferences.

There are three main types, each serving a different purpose.

A forensic autopsy (also called a medicolegal autopsy) is ordered by legal authorities — such as a medical examiner, a coroner, or a court — when a death is suspicious, violent, legally significant, or otherwise requires official investigation. Its results may be used in criminal or civil court proceedings.

A clinical autopsy (also called a hospital autopsy) is performed in a hospital or medical setting, usually with the written consent of the deceased person's family, to understand a disease better or to verify a medical diagnosis made before death. Its primary purpose is medical understanding, not legal investigation.

A research autopsy is performed specifically to advance scientific knowledge — to study how a particular disease affects the body, to investigate a new medical phenomenon, or to contribute to medical literature. These are always done with proper consent.

Government officials such as a medical examiner or coroner have the legal authority to order an autopsy without the family's consent, particularly when the death falls into a legally defined category requiring investigation. Hospitals can request a clinical autopsy, but they typically need the consent of the family or next of kin. Families themselves can also commission a private autopsy — hiring an independent pathologist at their own expense — if they are unsatisfied with official findings or want a second, independent opinion.

Once the examination is complete, the pathologist compiles an autopsy report — a formal, detailed written document that records every finding. It includes a physical description of the body, all abnormalities and injuries discovered, the weight and condition of each organ, microscopic findings, toxicology results, and the official conclusions about the cause and manner of death. This report is a legal and medical document of significant importance. It can be used in court cases, submitted to insurance companies, included in public health records, or shared with the deceased person's family.

An autopsy is only ever performed on someone who has already died — it is never performed on a living person. It is also different from surgery: surgery aims to treat or heal a living patient, whereas an autopsy aims to investigate and understand a deceased one. While the process is invasive and technically complex, it is always performed with precision and professional respect for the deceased.

An autopsy is the scientific and medical examination of a dead human body. It is performed by a specially trained doctor called a pathologist, who examines the body inside and out — inspecting organs, studying tissues under a microscope, and testing body fluids — in order to determine why and how the person died, uncover any diseases or injuries, support legal investigations, and advance medical knowledge. The examination concludes with an official autopsy report, which documents all findings and records the cause and manner of death. It is one of the most powerful and reliable tools that medicine and law have for understanding death.

Autumn is one of the four seasons of the year. The four seasons, in order, are: spring → summer → autumn → winter. Autumn comes after summer and before winter. It is the third season of the year.

Think of the year as a full cycle. Summer is the peak — hot, long days, full bloom. Then, as if the world slowly exhales, things begin to wind down. That winding-down period is autumn.

This depends on where in the world you are.

In the Northern Hemisphere (countries like India, the UK, the USA, China, etc.):
Autumn roughly spans September, October, and November.

In the Southern Hemisphere (countries like Australia, Argentina, South Africa, etc.):
Autumn falls during March, April, and May — the opposite half of the year, because the seasons are reversed there.

(Today, October 11, 2026 — you are living through autumn right now, in India.)

Astronomically speaking, autumn officially begins on the autumnal equinox (around September 22–23 in the Northern Hemisphere) — the day when daytime and nighttime are nearly equal in length — and ends on the winter solstice (around December 21–22), the shortest day of the year.

Autumn is defined by a set of very real, observable changes in the natural world:

1. Temperatures drop.
The heat of summer fades. The air becomes cooler, sometimes crisp. You start reaching for a jacket.

2. Daylight shrinks.
The days grow shorter. The sun rises later and sets earlier. By the time autumn ends, in many places it gets dark surprisingly early in the evening.

3. Leaves change colour and fall.
This is perhaps autumn's most iconic feature. In many parts of the world, the leaves of trees transform from green into brilliant shades of red, orange, yellow, and brown. Then, they dry up and fall to the ground. This is why, in American English, the season is also called "fall" (see below).

4. Nature prepares for winter.
Animals begin storing food, migrating to warmer places, or preparing to hibernate. Plants go dormant. The natural world braces for the cold.

5. Harvest time.
Autumn has traditionally been the season when crops are gathered. Fruits, vegetables, and grains ripened over summer are collected before winter sets in. This is why autumn is deeply associated with abundance, harvest festivals, and gratitude in cultures around the world.

Yes, they refer to exactly the same season. The difference is purely one of dialect:

  • "Autumn" is the standard term used in British English and in formal writing worldwide.
  • "Fall" is the informal term used in American English.

You will hear an American say "I love the fall" and a British person say "I love the autumn" — they mean the same thing entirely. In international or academic writing, "autumn" is generally preferred.

Beyond the literal season, "autumn" is also used metaphorically to describe a period of late maturity, gradual decline, or approaching end — the stage before something fades out completely, much like how autumn precedes winter.

Examples:

  • "He was in the autumn of his life" — meaning he was in old age, the later years of his life, before death.
  • "The autumn of the empire" — meaning the empire was past its peak and slowly declining.

This figurative use works because autumn, in nature, is beautiful but bittersweet — things are at their most colourful, and yet they are also dying. Writers and speakers borrow this image to describe human experiences with a similar quality: rich, mature, but drawing to a close.
How "autumn" is used grammatically as a noun

As a noun, "autumn" can be used in several ways:

As a general/uncountable reference (no article needed):

  • "I love autumn."
  • "In autumn, the leaves turn red."
  • "This happens every autumn."

With the definite article "the":

  • "The autumn of 2025 was unusually warm."
  • "We met in the autumn."

(Using "the" is common when referring to a specific autumn, or simply as a matter of style — both "in autumn" and "in the autumn" are correct.)

As a countable noun (when talking about multiple autumns):

  • "I have spent five autumns in London."
  • "It was one of the most beautiful autumns I can remember."

As a modifier (when "autumn" describes another noun):
While this shifts it toward adjective-like use, it is still functioning as a noun modifying another noun:

  • "autumn leaves" — the leaves of autumn
  • "autumn breeze" — the breeze of autumn
  • "autumn harvest" — the harvest that happens in autumn
Common words and phrases associated with "autumn"

These collocations will help you use and recognize "autumn" naturally:

  • early/mid/late autumn — referring to the beginning, middle, or end of the season
  • autumn leaves — the colourful leaves that fall from trees
  • autumn colours — the red, orange, and gold tones of the season
  • autumn equinox — the astronomical start of autumn
  • autumn harvest — the gathering of crops in autumn
  • autumnal — the adjective form, meaning "of or relating to autumn" ("autumnal colours," "an autumnal mood")
The emotional and cultural weight of autumn

Autumn carries a strong emotional resonance in literature, art, and everyday life. It is often described as:

  • Melancholic — because things are dying and the cold is coming
  • Beautiful — because of the spectacular colours
  • Cosy — because of warm drinks, blankets, and shorter days spent indoors
  • Reflective — a time to look back before a new cycle begins

This is why you will encounter "autumn" frequently in poetry and literature as a symbol of change, transition, beauty in decline, and the passage of time.

If you had to define it in one sentence:

Autumn is the season of the year that follows summer and precedes winter, marked by falling temperatures, shorter days, and — most visually — the changing and falling of leaves.

Everything else above is the full, living texture of what that single season truly means.
1319:
Autumnal is an adjective that means of, relating to, or characteristic of autumn. It describes anything that belongs to autumn, feels like autumn, or reminds you of autumn.

But there is more to it than that. The word does two distinct jobs — one literal, one figurative — and understanding both is what truly mastering this word looks like.

When used literally, autumnal describes things that are actually present in or associated with the autumn season — the sights, sounds, smells, and feelings of that time of year.

Think of:

  • Colour: The reds, oranges, golds, and browns of dying leaves. You would call them autumnal colours or an autumnal palette.
  • Weather: The crisp, cool air, the shorter days, the grey skies. You would call it autumnal weather or an autumnal chill.
  • Light: Autumn light is lower in the sky, softer, and more golden than summer light. You would call it autumnal light.
  • Mood: The quiet, slower pace of the season. You would call it an autumnal atmosphere.

Examples:

"The park looked beautiful, dressed in autumnal shades of red and gold."
"There was an autumnal bite to the morning air."
"The photographer loved the soft, autumnal light of October afternoons."
The Figurative Use — and This Is the Heart of the Word

Here is where autumnal becomes truly rich and interesting.

Autumn is the season that comes after summer's peak. It is a time of beauty, but also of things fading, slowing down, and drawing to a close. Leaves are gorgeous precisely because they are dying. The days are pleasant, but you can feel winter coming.

Because of this, autumnal is widely used as a metaphor for the later stages of something — particularly the later stages of a human life. Just as autumn follows summer and precedes winter, a person's autumnal years are their middle to later years: past the peak of youth, full of a certain depth and wisdom, but also edging toward an ending.

Examples:

"In his autumnal years, he spent more time reading and reflecting than chasing ambition."
"There was an autumnal quality to her thinking — mature, measured, and a little melancholic."
"The empire was in its autumnal phase: still powerful, but clearly past its height."

This figurative use extends beyond people. You can describe a civilisation, a career, a relationship, an era as autumnal — meaning it is in a late, fading, reflective stage.
The Mood and Feeling the Word Carries

Even when neither literally nor figuratively referring to the season or old age, autumnal carries a very specific emotional tone. That tone includes:

  • Wistfulness — a gentle longing for something past
  • Melancholy — not deep sadness, but a quiet, bittersweet ache
  • Reflection — a tendency to look back rather than forward
  • Beauty mixed with transience — something lovely precisely because it will not last

If a novelist calls a scene autumnal, even if it is set in spring, they are telling you to feel that mood: something is beautiful, something is fading, something is being mourned quietly.

Autumnal is not an everyday, conversational word. You would not typically say to a friend, "It's autumnal outside, isn't it?" — you would more naturally say "It feels like autumn" or "It's very fall-like."

Autumnal belongs to formal, literary, and descriptive writing — novels, essays, poetry, quality journalism, and literary criticism. It is the kind of word a writer reaches for when they want precision, elegance, and depth all at once.

Choosing autumnal over simply saying autumn (as a noun used as a modifier, e.g., "autumn colours") signals that the writer is being deliberate and literary. It elevates the description. It invites the reader to feel the full emotional weight of the season, not just identify it.

DimensionWhat it means

Autumnal is an adjective with layers. On the surface, it means relating to or characteristic of autumn. Literally, it describes colours, weather, light, and feelings that belong to the season. Figuratively, it describes the later, quieter, reflective stages of a life, an era, or anything that has passed its peak and is heading toward an end. Emotionally, it always carries a note of beauty tinged with sadness, of things that are lovely because they are fading. And stylistically, it is a formal, literary word — one used with care, chosen for its elegance and its power to evoke a whole world of feeling in a single adjective.
One Final Way to Remember It

Whenever you see autumnal, ask yourself: Does this feel like an October afternoon — beautiful, a little cool, a little sad, and glowing with a warmth that you know will not last much longer?

If the answer is yes, the word is being used exactly right.
